title: Too Busy to Notice You're Busy? Do a Time Audit
hook: Most of us can't say where our hours actually go. Writing them down for a few days is a blunt, effective way to find out — and to reclaim some.
key_points: A time audit means recording how you actually spend your hours, not how you think you do.
The gap between the two is usually the surprise — and the opportunity.
Psychotherapist Niro Feliciano recommends it for people who feel busy without knowing why.
The point isn't efficiency; it's making room for what actually matters to you.
It's a low-cost exercise: a notebook and a few honest days.
content_html: Some busyness is real and some is a fog — you end the day drained without being able to say what consumed it. Psychotherapist Niro Feliciano, speaking to NPR, suggests a plain remedy: write down what you actually did, hour by hour, for a few days.
extra_html:
That's the whole exercise. No app required — a notebook and enough honesty to log the twenty minutes on your phone alongside the meetings. What makes it work is the gap it exposes. Almost everyone carries a rough mental model of where their time goes, and almost everyone's model is wrong in a specific, personal way. Seeing the real distribution is what makes it possible to change.

Feliciano frames the goal as making room for what matters, not wringing more output from the day. That distinction matters if you're already stretched: a time audit used as a productivity whip just adds pressure. Used as a priorities check, it tends to surface one or two recoverable hours a week — which is usually enough to put something back that you'd quietly dropped.

related.title: Spotting and Beating Burnout
related.hook: Burnout isn't just being tired — it's exhaustion, cynicism, and feeling ineffective, and it comes from chronic stress you haven't been able to offload.

related.title: Building Everyday Resilience
related.hook: Resilience isn't a personality you're born with — it's a set of habits and connections you can build, the way you build a muscle.

related.title: Building Healthier Screen Habits
related.hook: You don't need to quit your phone — just out-design it. A few small tweaks beat willpower for taking back your attention.

flashcards.back_html: Recording how you actually spend your hours over a few days — rather than relying on your impression of where the time goes.

flashcards.prompt: What is the goal of a time audit, according to Feliciano?

choices.text: To spot what's wasting your time and make room for what matters
To squeeze maximum productivity out of every hour
To prove you have no free time at all

flashcards.explanation_html: The exercise is about priorities, not efficiency — finding the drains so you can redirect that time toward things you actually care about.
